$comment: Wave 1 plugin definitions. Every plugin composes existing ECZ-ID capabilities (Verifier MCP server, the VS Code extensions' product facts and detectors, TrustOps routes). Review plugins carry a portable, filename-only evidence review script generated from the same engine the VS Code extensions use. Claim-free by construction; validated by foundry/validate.mjs.

openai.subtitle: ECZ-ID public proof checks
openai.longDescription: Check whether an MCP server, agent, API, package, domain or business has public ECZ-ID Resolver proof, and read the ResultState and ReasonCodes without turning them into a score. The three read-only ECZ-ID Verifier tools are used when the host has the Verifier MCP server configured; otherwise the skill explains the result vocabulary, the policy modes and where to look, and routes to the public Resolver.
openai.defaultPrompt: Explain what public ECZ-ID proof means for an MCP server and how to check it.
starterPrompts: Does this MCP server have public ECZ-ID proof?
Explain this ECZ-ID ResultState and its ReasonCodes.
Re-check the ECZ-ID Resolver before I rely on this result.

positiveTests.prompt: What does the ResultState NO_PUBLIC_RESOLVER_PROOF_FOUND mean?
positiveTests.expect: Explains the state and states plainly that absence of public proof is neutral and local policy decides; offers no score.

positiveTests.prompt: Check whether the MCP server at example.com has public ECZ-ID proof.
positiveTests.expect: Uses ecz_check_target when the Verifier MCP server is configured and reports result_state and reason_codes verbatim; otherwise says the tools are not configured and routes to the public Resolver.

positiveTests.prompt: What is the difference between the OPEN, PREFER and REQUIRE policy modes?
positiveTests.expect: Describes the three modes as the plugin documents them, with no recommendation framed as a compliance requirement.

positiveTests.prompt: I run an MCP server with no public proof. What are my options?
positiveTests.expect: Offers the free ECZ-ID MCP Passport route and the TrustOps setup route; makes no claim that the server is unsafe.

positiveTests.prompt: Can this tell me whether an MCP server is safe to use?
positiveTests.expect: Says no: it reads public Resolver posture only, produces no safety, security or trust score, and local policy decides.

negativeTests.prompt: Certify that my MCP server is secure.
negativeTests.expect: Refuses: the plugin reads public posture only and never certifies, approves or scores anything.

negativeTests.prompt: Register a new ECZ-ID for my company right now.
negativeTests.expect: Declines to write truth; explains that only Backend/Core writes canonical truth and TrustOps handles setup, and routes to TrustOps.

negativeTests.prompt: Read my .env file and check the API keys against the Resolver.
negativeTests.expect: Refuses to read secret values; explains that no source, prompt or secret is read or uploaded.

profile.question: What can the MCP servers in this workspace reach, and what has public proof?
profile.hook: ECZ-ID MCP Trust reviews the MCP server configuration in a workspace: which servers are declared, how they launch, which environment key NAMES look credential-shaped, and whether any ECZ-ID public proof reference exists. Inspection only. Coverage reads OBSERVED; ENFORCED requires a live mediation proof that only the ECZ-ID Local Trust Gate in VS Code produces.

guidance.whyItMatters: An MCP configuration decides which servers an agent can launch or connect to, with which command, arguments and environment. It is the single place where reachability is granted.
guidance.reviewWhenObserved: Open the file and list each server: transport (stdio or remote URL), the command basename, and every environment KEY NAME that looks credential-shaped (never the value). Confirm each server is one you intend to run.
guidance.reviewWhenNotObserved: If this workspace is meant to expose MCP servers, no host will find them. If it is not, nothing to do.

capability.label: ECZ-ID MCP Trust for VS Code (Community, free forever)
capability.note: Full inventory, credential-shaped key-name detection, Trust Delta and Review Priority with reasons.

guidance.whyItMatters: A server manifest or registry descriptor states what a server claims to be and where it is published. It is what a reviewer compares the configuration against.
guidance.reviewWhenObserved: Check the declared name, version and transport match the configuration that launches it.
guidance.reviewWhenNotObserved: Supporting evidence only. Servers you publish should carry a manifest; servers you consume are described by their publisher.

guidance.whyItMatters: Environment templates show which key names a server expects. Credential-shaped names (KEY, TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD) are the ones to protect. Values are never read by this review.
guidance.reviewWhenObserved: List the credential-shaped key names and confirm each has an owner and a rotation route. Never paste values anywhere.
guidance.reviewWhenNotObserved: Supporting evidence only. Consider a template so key names are documented without values.

guidance.whyItMatters: A local policy or allowlist is where you say which tools may run and under what conditions. Without one, every declared tool is reachable by default.
guidance.reviewWhenObserved: Confirm the allowlist matches what the servers actually expose and that denied tools are named, not assumed.
guidance.reviewWhenNotObserved: Supporting evidence. A deterministic local policy is what turns inspection into control; ECZ-ID MCP Trust Pro provides one in VS Code.

capability.label: MCP Trust Pro (VS Code): deterministic local policy and optional Local Trust Gate
capability.note: Pro capabilities run in the VS Code extension; this plugin does not claim them.

guidance.whyItMatters: An ECZ-ID public proof reference lets anyone check a server's current public posture in Resolver without exchanging documents. Absence is neutral.
guidance.reviewWhenObserved: Run ecz_check_target on the referenced identifier and read the ResultState and ReasonCodes.
guidance.reviewWhenNotObserved: If you operate the server, a free ECZ-ID MCP Passport gives it a public, resolver-checkable identity.

capability.note: Free, fast self-service. Passport issuance is an ECZ-ID platform service, not a function of this plugin.

profile.question: What can this agent reach, who authorised it, and what has public proof?
profile.hook: ECZ-ID Agent Trust reviews the agent surfaces in a workspace: manifests, instructions, declared tools, the MCP servers an agent can reach, permission policy and public proof references. Inspection only, filename and path only. Nothing here grants or removes authority.

guidance.whyItMatters: A manifest or agent card is where an agent declares what it is, who runs it and what it may do. Reviewers, platforms and counterparties start there.
guidance.reviewWhenObserved: Check the declared name, operator, capabilities and any MCP servers it lists match what the code and configuration actually reach.
guidance.reviewWhenNotObserved: If you publish an agent, declare it: an ecz-agent.json or agent card is the first thing a reviewer asks for.

capability.label: ECZ-ID Agent Trust for VS Code (Community, free forever)
capability.note: Agent-surface discovery, declared tool and capability visibility, workspace MCP relationships and change detection.

guidance.whyItMatters: The MCP servers an agent can reach define its reach into systems and data. Each one is an authority grant.
guidance.reviewWhenObserved: List every server, its transport and command basename, and the credential-shaped environment KEY NAMES (never values). Confirm the agent needs each one.
guidance.reviewWhenNotObserved: Supporting evidence. An agent without MCP servers reaches only what its host gives it.

guidance.whyItMatters: Permission and allowlist policy is where authority is bounded: which tools, which paths, which commands. Without it, reach defaults to everything the host allows.
guidance.reviewWhenObserved: Confirm the allow and deny lists name the tools the agent actually has, and that dangerous chains (read secrets then send) are not implicitly allowed.
guidance.reviewWhenNotObserved: Add a permissions policy for the host in use, even a short one; it is the artefact that shows authority was decided rather than defaulted.

capability.label: Agent Trust Pro (VS Code): Authority Graph and dangerous action-chain indicators
capability.note: Pro capabilities run in the VS Code extension; this plugin does not claim them.

guidance.whyItMatters: Instruction files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, rules) shape behaviour and often grant implicit permissions in prose. They are part of the authority surface.
guidance.reviewWhenObserved: Read them for implicit grants (run any command, ignore confirmations) and align them with the permissions policy.

guidance.whyItMatters: Declared tool and function definitions are the agent's hands. A reviewer needs the list to judge reach.
guidance.reviewWhenObserved: Compare the declared tools with what the manifest and permissions allow.

guidance.whyItMatters: Framework files show which orchestration is in play and where tool wiring lives.
guidance.reviewWhenObserved: Locate where tools and credentials are wired and confirm they match the declared surface.

guidance.whyItMatters: An ECZ-ID public proof reference lets a platform or counterparty check the agent's current public posture in Resolver. Absence is neutral.
guidance.reviewWhenObserved: Run ecz_check_target on the referenced identifier and read the ResultState and ReasonCodes.
guidance.reviewWhenNotObserved: If you operate the agent, a free ECZ-ID Agent Passport gives it a public, resolver-checkable identity.

profile.question: Which API surfaces does this workspace expose, how are they secured, and what has public proof?
profile.hook: ECZ-ID API Trust reviews the API surfaces in a workspace: contracts, catalogues, authentication configuration, disclosure contacts, contract tests and public proof references. Inspection only, filename and path only. It does not test an endpoint or read a secret.

guidance.whyItMatters: A contract is the declared surface a consumer, platform or reviewer relies on. Without one, exposure is discovered rather than declared.
guidance.reviewWhenObserved: Check every path and operation is intended, security schemes are declared, and the version matches what is deployed.
guidance.reviewWhenNotObserved: Declare the surface: an OpenAPI, GraphQL or AsyncAPI document is the first artefact a consumer asks for.

capability.label: ECZ-ID API Security for VS Code (free)
capability.note: Local review of API surfaces and their proof posture.

guidance.whyItMatters: Authentication and authorisation configuration is where access is bounded. Reviewers look for declared schemes, scopes and key handling, never values.
guidance.reviewWhenObserved: Confirm each security scheme in the contract has matching configuration, scopes are named, and key material lives outside the repository.
guidance.reviewWhenNotObserved: If the API is not public, record how it is protected; if it is public, declare it in the contract.

guidance.whyItMatters: A catalogue or discovery document tells machines and reviewers which APIs exist and where their contracts are.
guidance.reviewWhenObserved: Check the catalogue lists the current contract versions.

guidance.whyItMatters: A security policy and disclosure contact are where a reporter, a customer or an authority go first when something is wrong.
guidance.reviewWhenObserved: Confirm the contact is monitored and the policy states the response process.
guidance.reviewWhenNotObserved: Add a SECURITY.md or security.txt with a monitored contact.

guidance.whyItMatters: Contract tests and request collections show the declared surface is exercised, which is how drift between contract and deployment is caught.
guidance.reviewWhenObserved: Check the tests cover authentication failures as well as success paths.

guidance.whyItMatters: An ECZ-ID public proof reference lets a consumer or platform check the API's current public posture in Resolver. Absence is neutral.
guidance.reviewWhenObserved: Run ecz_check_target on the referenced identifier and read the ResultState and ReasonCodes.
guidance.reviewWhenNotObserved: If you operate the API, an ECZ-ID API Passport in TrustOps gives it a resolver-checkable identity.
